overview.headline: How wing size changes lift for flight

keyPoints.point: lift generated by an object depends on size and surrounding air motion
keyPoints.quote: The amount of lift generated by an object depends on the size of the object.

keyPoints.point: lift acts as force component perpendicular to flight direction
keyPoints.quote: Lift is the component of this force perpendicular to the flight direction.

keyPoints.point: lift is directly proportional to area so larger wing surface gives more lift
keyPoints.quote: Like the other aerodynamic force, drag, the lift is directly proportional to the area of the object.

keyPoints.point: designers increase wing area to keep lift high during low velocity takeoff and landing
keyPoints.quote: Takeoff and landing are times of relatively low velocity, so to keep the lift high (to avoid the ground!) designers try to increase the wing area.

keyTerms.gloss: aerodynamic force acting perpendicular to flight direction
keyTerms.quote: Lift is an aerodynamic force and therefore depends on the pressure variation of the air around the body as it moves through the air.

keyTerms.gloss: other aerodynamic force mentioned alongside lift
keyTerms.quote: Like the other aerodynamic force, drag, the lift is directly proportional to the area of the object.

keyTerms.gloss: flat wing area viewed from above along lift direction
keyTerms.quote: The planform area is the area of the wing as viewed from above the wing, looking along the “lift” direction.

keyTerms.gloss: movable sections slid backwards to increase wing area
keyTerms.quote: This is done by sliding the flaps backwards along metal tracks and shifting the slats forward to increase the wing area.
